articleTitle: Communications: Single-sideband transmission for land mobile radio: From seven to ten times as many channels could be made available in existing VHF and UHF bands
abstract: Existing mobile radio bands could be used more effectively to accommodate more traffic in the same bandwidth. With available technologies, from seven to ten times as many channels could be obtained in existing VHF and UHF bands, states a recent study for the UHF Task Force of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission.

articleTitle: Power/energy: New York City's blackout: A $350 million drain: Ripple effects off the July 13, 1977, lightning stroke cost the public dearly in lost property, services, end income
abstract: The New York City blackout of July 14, 1977 (Feb., p. 38; Mar., p. 48) cost the city and its inhabitants more than $350 million, according to a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) report released this past July.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: How VLSI impacts computer architecture: A solution is suggested to the imminent problem of having more computer intelligence on a chip than anyone can use
abstract: In this article Dr. Faggin suggests a specific direction for a future VLSI architecture that his company, Zilog, Inc., will implement. The reader is cautioned that the author is offering his personal views on a controversial area in which many authorities feel there are still no well-defined answers. — Ed.

articleTitle: Education: A radical experiment in teaching
abstract: Describes Worcester Polytechnic Institute's nontraditional approach to education. It is based on self-initiated study, terminal accountability, and undergraduate projects-rather than courses-as the heart of the learning experience. The school has only four academic requirements for graduation-three projects, and competency examination.

articleTitle: Energy: Industrial energy control: The computer takes charge: Limited intelligence will suffice for local control, but computers are needed for overall system control
abstract: Everyone knows that managing our energy-related activities is essential, but the need is particularly great for industry. Steel and aluminum plants are highly energy intensive, and pulp and paper processing consumes more power per ton of output than any other major industry. Especially in these vital areas, energy management must be effective and, toward that end, will require multilevel controls.

articleTitle: How energy, and its cost, enter the `productivity equation'
abstract: Energy use, economic growth, and average labor productivity are closely related to one another, and an analysis of these relationships in the United States shows that the next decade is Likely to be one of reduced rate of growth of labor productivity, accompanied by a lowered rate of economic growth. These reductions can be traced to the fourfold increase in petroleum prices in late 1973 and early 1974.

articleTitle: Biomedical: For diabetics: An electronic pancreas: A bionic device implanted below the human diaphragm will deliver insulin into the peritoneum and be inductively programmable
abstract: My wife and I returned to Albuquerque from San Francisco on a Saturday afternoon at the conclusion of WESCON. We knew that our youngest daughter was ill. Her illness has been diagnosed as a simple viral infection and she had been left in the care of her grandmother. When we saw her, we were shocked. She had lost about 15 pounds, was hyperventilating, the muscles in her face were in convulsion, and she was unable to keep down any food or liquids. We immediately called our physician, who reconfirmed his initial diagnosis and told us not to be alarmed. At about 5:00 a.m. on Sunday, we rushed her to the emergency ward of the local hospital. By this time, she was completely unintelligible. Two hours later, her condition was diagnosed as diabetes with an extremely high blood-sugar level. Immediate treatment with insulin and intravenous fluid injections was begun. It took another 48 hours before our daughter's blood-glucose level began to approach normal and she regained consciousness.

articleTitle: Solid state: CCD and bubble memories system implications: Mainframe computers and intelligent terminals are predicted to be primary beneficiaries
abstract: For many years, an “access gap” existed between fast electronic memories (< 1-µs access time) and the slower magnetic serial-access memories (> 5×103-µs access time), a gap that was not to be bridged until the mid-1970s with the emergence of viable cost-effective new electronic technologies — electron-beam addressable memories (EBAMs), charge-coupled-device (CCD) memories, and magnetic-bubble memories (MBMs). Now, price/performance tradeoffs for these memory technologies have led to several new options in computer architecture, as will be shown here for the case of CCDs and MBMs.

articleTitle: Robots quietly take their place alongside humans on the production line to raise productivity-and do the 'dirty work'
abstract: Contemporary robots do not at all resemble science-fiction humanoids. But they can do much of the work still performed largely by humans, even in plants filled with automated heavy machinery. They can handle materials, load and unload, sort, stack, and do assembly operations. They can position workpieces on machines. They weld, spray, rivet, ladle, rout, sand, and grind. They can do many of the monotonous, hot, disagreeable, dangerous tasks formerly assigned to humans, as well as new tasks that humans can't do. They can work for thousands of hours with, typically, less than 2-percent downtime. Humans can reprogram robots to different tasks by literally leading them by the hand through the new routines. And the digital electronics of their control systems places them squarely on the computer-aided manufacturing scene of the near future.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Landing aircraft under poor conditions: Time-reference scanning beams characterize the all-weather microwave landing system that will replace present systems
abstract: Last April, a divisional meeting of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) settled upon a new all-weather landing system that will eventually replace the present instrument landing system (ILS) for aircraft. The choice of the United States/Australian time-reference scanning-beam microwave landing system (TRSB MLS) ended a selection process that started ten years ago in the U.S., and six years ago in ICAO, that, as the box on page 54 indicates, was not without controversy and debate.

articleTitle: The engineer: The engineer and public policy-making: Like a gladiator with one arm bound behind him, the engineer enters the public arena handicapped by personality and training
abstract: During the French Revolution, a priest, a lawyer, and an engineer were put on trial as enemies of the Revolution. The priest tried to defend himself by explaining how he had ministered to the poor, brought food to the hungry, and tended the sick. To no avail. He was sentenced to the guillotine. In those days, when a person felt he had been sentenced unjustly, he would demonstrate his feelings by making the supreme gesture — he would lie face up rather than face down in the guillotine. The priest did so. When the rope was tripped, it happened that the blade stuck in the channel about six inches above his neck. It was the rule that if ever the guillotine stuck, the victim was let free. So the priest was spared.

articleTitle: Power: Harnessing the wind: New schemes may provide solutions to the age-old problem of building efficient wind machines
abstract: Wind energy presents many advantages. It is clean, free, renewable, and domestically produced. And now, with the aid of modern technology, it could be used to a greater extent than ever before to offset U.S. dependence on imported oil. As much as 20 to 40 percent of the nation's total energy supply could be provided by wind-energy generating systems.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Helping speeders beat the radar rap: Moving radar and dual-band detectors constitute a miniature ECM race between enforcement-minded authorities and motoring outlaws
abstract: Radar for catching speeders has been around since the late 1940s. But now U.S. motorists are really beginning to feel the “pinch” with the advent of two recent developments: the 55-mi/h national speed limit, and “moving” radar that allows police cars to single out speeding drivers while maintaining normal patrol of highways (no need to hide bulky equipment along the roadside and tie up another officer). And as police efficiency has risen, so too has the demand for a reliable radar detector that gives advance warning of an impending summons. Dozens of new “garage shop” companies have attempted to produce a workable, low-cost detector, and a handful (so far) have succeeded. These small microwave receivers work at signal levels that would challenge the resolving power of a laboratory spectrum analyzer, yet they are priced around $100 each. And the legality of detector use and ownership is becoming more widespread as those few state/local laws that outlaw the device crumble in court.

articleTitle: Power: MHD's target: Payoff by 2000: Efficiencies over 50 percent and generating costs of 32 mills/kWh may make magnetohydrodynamic systems viable by 1995
abstract: The magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) technique for generating electricity involves the interaction between a magnetic field and a conducting medium that is fluid rather than solid, as in conventional generators. MHD germinated more than a century ago, but now the attempt to translate it into a viable, commercially acceptable energy-conversion technology is intensifying as a result of the need to improve the use of fuel resources that are being depleted. The United States, for example, plans to have an operational pilot plant as early as 1985, and a base-load commercial demonstration plant before 1995.

articleTitle: Computers: Microcomputers promise less stop, more go: Designers off urban traffic-control systems propose hierarchical schemes to enhance local control, reliability, and maintainability
abstract: Spurred by the dramatic increase in the number of vehicles using — and clogging — the streets of today's cities, urban traffic control has undergone various technological changes in recent years in the drive toward greater functionality and efficiency, and more cost-effective equipment. Thus, traffic-control equipment has evolved from electromechanical intersection controllers, through electronic units, to systems employing minicomputers. The recent stage in this evolutionary process is the introduction of microcomputer-based systems.

articleTitle: Inventors: `Protect thyself': Careful attention to the claims section will go far toward establishing patent validity and extending the scope of protection
abstract: The single most important reason why so many electrical patents are of dubious value is that inventors fail to participate fully in the task of patent preparation. The vast majority of inventors carefully review drawings and descriptions before their patent applications are filed. But unfortunately, an almost equal proportion totally ignore the claims section (one-paragraph summaries of the invention), with the excuse that they are legal jargon and, therefore, incomprehensible in the first place. These engineers overlook the fact that the validity of the patent and the scope of the protection are measured by the claims. The most accurate and thorough description will be of no avail, and would-be infringers will be able to "design around the patent," if the claims do not succinctly set forth the crux of the invention.

No modern television facility, operating in a competitive world, can ignore the obvious advantages offered by the new breed of one-inch helical video-tape recorders that are currently available for high-quality studio program production, portable field use, and post-production editing. These new helicals also offer considerable benefits as replacement machines for the TV broadcast centers whose two-inch quadruplex VTRs have been fully amortized.

articleTitle: Productivity IV: What can Government do?
abstract: Government clout, when used wisely, can have an extremely positive effect on productivity. The problem is that there is no clear-cut pain to efficacy of government influence for that purpose. What looks wise in retrospect may have been, at the time of decision, no more or less brilliant than other comparable decisions that proved to be ineffective, or even adverse. In fact, as author Nash points out in the following article, government influence is frequently ignored because major technological innovation - and the attendant productivity improvement - do look so simple in retrospect.

articleTitle: Consumers as programmers: TV networks are upstaged by VCRs and video games; turnkey personal computers plunge in price
abstract: Video tape for the home has been vindicated! Despite a decade of rumors, promises, and abortive new product introductions, consumers are now offered two well-designed (but incompatible) video cassette systems marketed under a dozen different brand names. And all these video cassette machines are reportedly brisk sellers, commanding retail prices of around $1000 each.

articleTitle: Patents: The patentability of software inventions: Computer-implemented inventions that are useful, new, and nonobvious may still not be patentable - except, say courts, in certain cases
abstract: Are the originators of computer inventions entitled to patent protection? The answer to this question, which has spawned considerable confusion, controversy, and debate, depends on the answer to a related question: Is the programming of digital computers one of the useful arts? If the answer is no, an entire technological field may be excluded from the benefits of the patent system.

articleTitle: NSF's three-phase program helps the small-business innovator bootstrap an idea to commercial success
abstract: A new National Science Foundation (NSF) program, introduced in part as a result of interest on the part of the U.S. Congress, has among its objectives greater utilization of small science and technology firms in U.S. Government R&D, and conversion of that research to technological innovation in the private sector. Called “Small Business Innovation Applied to National Needs,” the new program solicits high-risk, potentially high-payoff, proposals from small business relating to the research objectives of the Applied Science and Research Applications (ASRA) Directorate.

articleTitle: Microcomputers: For Detroit: Smaller and smarter chips: Semiconductor manufacturers are designing more complex microcomputer systems, while they, and the auto makers, worry about reliability
abstract: Now that automobile manufacturers throughout the world have relatively complex microprocessor systems in production cars, semiconductor houses are readying the next round of goodies for automotive application. With predictions of one million devices per chip by 1985, semiconductor manufacturers are thinking about such things as single-chip engine and power-train control microcomputers. But even sooner than the mid-1980s, devices such as EEPROMS (electrically erasable programmable read-only memories) — sometimes called EAROMS (electrically alterable read-only memories) — will offer an ability to modify stored-data tables and calibrations so that self-tuning engines will be possible. Such engines will use different calibrations as they age and will “remember” how hard they have been accelerated and decelerated during various engine conditions.

Jobs are at stake, some say. Our very quality of life is in jeopardy. The speakers are no mere prophets of doom; their growing ranks include leaders of government, industry, and academia as well as social and physical scientists and, last but not least, engineers. The common target of their concern is productivity.

articleTitle: Introducing a revolutionary new Home Learning Center: The new Encyclopaedia Britannica Program at a substantially reduced price!

abstract: Denying press characterizations of radicalism, S. David Freeman, new chairman of the Tennessee Valley Authority, tells Spectrum his plans.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Emphasis on field: Microprocessor-based systems spawn built-in test gear
abstract: Currently there is an urgent need for more effective instruments to handle increasingly complex microprocessor-based data-processing equipment in the field. Whether they make an instrument, subassembly, or a large computer complex, manufacturers of equipment are under constant pressure to offer more serviceable products, because higher service costs are taking bigger bites out of profit margins for both manufacturers and users. As a result, instrument makers are churning out an array of such gear, using a variety of different techniques for troubleshooting.
For more information on the following products, circle numbers on the Reader Service Card corresponding to bracketed numbers.

articleTitle: Communications and microwave technology: Optical fibers compete with premium coax; digital radio reaches cost effectiveness
abstract: The “glamour” of communications research and development efforts continues to involve fiber optics. Laboratories in Europe, Japan, and the U.S. report considerable progress in reducing fiber costs, while increasing the data rates that optical transmitter/receiver links can handle. The ultimate goal, of course, is a low-cost glass-fiber replacement for copper conductors. Standard-grade bare fiber (10-dB loss at 200 MHz over 1 km) presently sells for 90€/meter, and costs are dropping fast.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The perils of publishing
abstract: "No force has been so influential in promoting the rapid progress of our profession and our industry as the hardwon fight to publish." Although these words were spoken in 1978,* they refer to a privilege that was forged in some heat and argument in the early days of our profession (circa 1912, when the American Institute of Electrical Engineers was coming to grips with the creation of a code of ethics).

articleTitle: Consumer: Video tape: Options for the buyer: Despite competing tape speeds, cassette sizes, and recording formats, the public is buying players, cameras, timers, and software
abstract: Video cassette tape recording (VCR) machines that can capture television programs off the air, or even preserve the antics of friends and children in all-electronic “home movies,” have snagged the imagination (and discretionary income) of consumers everywhere. Certainly no surprise development, consumer VCRs had been “promised” for over a decade. But until last year's introduction of several long-playing, compact consoles priced at $1000 or less, video tape had failed miserably with the buying public. The reasons were plain enough: high prices, complexity, sheer bulk of equipment, and short recording lime (half an hour at most on some early models).

articleTitle: Power: Evaluating system reliability: When, why, and how often do power systems fail? Such knowledge is invaluable in increasing uptime while holding costs in line
abstract: Obtaining the right relationship between a power system's reliability — namely, its ability to provide a continuous supply to its customers — and the system's cost has been a target of power system planners for a number of decades. And this objective still serves as a major motivation for the development of quantitative techniques for evaluating power system reliability. All three sectors of the system “ generation, transmission, and distribution “ are of interest. However, the biggest challenge is the transmission sector — which, unlike its generation and distribution counterparts, does not lend itself to straightforward analysis. (The structure of a power system was discussed by Donald Ewart in his article, “Whys and wherefores of power system blackouts,” Apr., p. 36.)

articleTitle: Patents: U.S. lags in patent law reform: The employed inventor in countries other than the U.S. often is given better incentives to create, plus greater statutory protection
abstract: In most major industrialized countries, an employee retains considerable rights in his or her inventions. The trend worldwide is toward legislation that limits the rights companies can extract as a condition of employment. Great Britain enacted such legislation just last year.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: In praise of objectivity
abstract: More and more frequently, the profession of engineering is finding itself called upon to address issues that are value-laden instead of factual. One supposes that all callings are subject to this demand to a greater or lesser extent. Yet it is disconcerting to observe the inability of the profession, in some cases, to deal with these new issues with equanimity and finesse. Of course, the very fact that these issues are value-laden suggests that subjectivity, not objectivity, will predominate.

articleTitle: Electronics to boost productivity: Computer technology spurs automation, energy cuts
abstract: Manufacturers are turning increasingly to electrical/electronics technologies for more efficient use of resources and higher productivity. Computers of all types are being employed for better plant and production-line management. For example: • Computer-run robots are beginning to appear on more assembly lines, doing more complicated tasks. • High-power industrial lasers for metal treating and other uses are becoming more feasible, and, together with infrared sensors, are helping to improve product quality. • Increased efficiency in such basic components as ac and dc motors and the use of power rectifiers (where semiconductors have replaced ignitrons) have increased both plant operating efficiencies and profit margins.

articleTitle: Education: Engineering curricula: `Professional' vs. `two-track': In the debate over possible changes in engineering education, one of the key questions is what is meant by `professional school'
abstract: Engineers in industry have complained frequently about the kind of engineering education that takes place in colleges today. Engineers in academe are quick to defend their accomplishments and poke holes in the arguments of their detractors. Much of the current debate centers around two proposals. The National Society of Professional Engineers (NSPE) has issued a call for 'professional schools of engineering' that are 'independent' (see box on p. 54). The other is a change to a two-track system that offers a four-year bachelor's degree in general engineering or a five-year practice-oriented master's that might be the first professional degree.

articleTitle: Electronic watchdogs for calls and copies
abstract: Recently, an insurance carrier discovered that an ingenious clerk was "capturing" an outbound WATS line each morning and using it as a surrogate babysitter for her young children. Her oldest child was trained to answer the telephone and then mount it in a nearby Speakerphone. The clerk would listen on the line for a second or so at frequent intervals throughout the day. If the children were fighting, an armistice was imposed by a whisper, amplified to a thunderous command by the Speakerphone. As soon as the children settled down, she would put the WATS line back on hold.

Obviously, productivity has come a long way from the village cobbler painstakingly handcrafting a pair of shoes “from the finest Spanish leather” for the lady of the manor. And although to some, the Chaplinesque production line represented on our front cover may have Orwellian implications of a dehumanized, mechanized life style, that same production line has meant that the many now can choose from a variety of goods that once were reserved to the elite few.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Distributed network fits in typewriter
abstract: Using three microprocessors rather than one costs less and makes for easier software development, say the designers of the new QYX word-processing typewriter. Their cost argument is based on the assumption that even if LSI die prices go to zero, the cost of chip packaging and board mounting comes out to a fixed price per pin. That being so, they feel they can get more intelligence with three 40-pin processors than with one 40-pin processor and two 40-pin peripheral I/O extenders.

articleTitle: Computers: Microcomputers invade the linear world: Analog interfacing techniques are in demand as microcomputers are exploited in inexpensive equipment for linear applications
abstract: The current low cost of microprocessors has justified their use in many areas, particularly in inexpensive equipment that previously could warrant only an analog approach to its implementation. As a result of these linear applications, there exists today a sizable demand for microprocessor analog interfaces — especially low-cost interfaces. These modern analog interfaces use a variety of techniques, geared to specific types of applications.

articleTitle: New product applications: CCD and CTD filters include tunable units and a spectrum analyzer on a chip
abstract: Said to be the first charge-transferdevice (CTD) filter family, this series of transversal filters includes two low-pass and two bandpass filters, each in a narrow- and a broad-band version.
For more information on the following products, circle numbers on the Reader Service Card corresponding to bracketed numbers.

articleTitle: Aerospace and military: Voyager begins planets rendezvous; improved night vision for the foot soldier
abstract: Electronics, and particularly solid-state circuitry, frequently have provided the springboard from which military and aerospace systems, large and small, have been advancing on a broad front.

articleTitle: New product applications: Single-board bipolar microcomputer emulates any mini- or microcomputer
abstract: The T-1000 is a single-board bipolar microcomputer that is designed for use in applications where software is available but computer operation is not fast enough or powerful enough for system expansion or new product development. It eliminates the cost and bother of new software and interface designs and can be microprogrammed to run the instruction set of any known minicomputer as well as any microcomputer.

articleTitle: Technology and society: While politicians struggle with communications and energy policy, GE `engineers' the perfect tomato
abstract: The heat generated at the interface between technology and society is by now expected. Less expected, but encouraging, are those moments when the sociotechnical interface produces light. Two of the "hottest" topics are energy and communications. In the United States, for example, there has been a continuing "battle of the advocates": in energy, among those pushing nuclear, those fighting it, the pro-solar cadres, the anti-solar forces, the environmentalists, the coal and oil lobbies, etc.; and in the area of communications, among the Bell System, the data-processing giants like IBM, and a raft of communications and data processing pygmies struggling to survive in a world of "Watusies."

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The New World Information Order: High stakes
abstract: Computers and communications technology are at the heart of a global problem affecting all countries, from the most to the least developed. Termed the “New World Information Order (NWIO),” its subject concerns the flow of news, entertainment, educational, and cultural information in its many formats across national boundaries.
For more information on the following products, circle numbers on the Reader Service Card corresponding to bracketed numbers.

articleTitle: Electronics and medicine: When electroquackery thrived: The mystery and glamor of electricity were exploited by charlatans who bilked the public with promises to cure any ill
abstract: Electroquackery has a history all its own that is as long and colorful as that of legitimate electromedicine. But then, the difference between serious research and outright fraud has often been a little unclear. At a time when electricity was only beginning to be understood, fakers proposed devices that seemed no stranger to the general public than the proposed devices of legitimate researchers, and the theories of even the most extravagant charlatan could gain a ready following because they hardly seemed less believable than the phenomena they were supposed to explain.

articleTitle: Applications literature: New methods for measuring return loss
abstract: This eight-page technical paper describes new, easy-to-use methods for accurately measuring reflected signals over the 5-MHz to 18-GHz range. The techniques discussed yield accuracies in measuring standing-wave ratios that were previously unobtainable, even with computer-aided systems.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: So you're an engineer. But what do you do?
abstract: Isn't it fascinating how over the years certain titles have proven to be so prestigious that they are often appropriated without the approval of officialdom, and, at times, downright misappropriated?

Do you suspect that they're talking behind your back - and you can't hear what they're saying? Now you can give yourself a comprehensive and relatively inexpensive hearing test in a matter of minutes, complete with a hard-copy printout of the results, by the simple push of a button. All you need for the audiogram is an instrument developed by Derek McClure of Alberta Systems Development Group, Wetaskiwin, Alta., Canada, and you're on your way.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: New philosophies for portable digital instruments: Signature analysis and circuit emulation are exploited in new test equipment to reduce runaway service costs
abstract: Paced by a maturing integrated-circuits technology, the costs of data-processing products have been declining steadily, which should be a bright note in the lives of computer and terminal-equipment manufacturers. But there is another, darker side to the coin — the rising cost of service and maintenance as the equipment increases in complexity and sophistication. And the problem is compounded by a lack of skilled service personnel, and by a spreading nontechnical data-processing customer base (banks, brokerage houses, retail outlets) that demands minimum equipment downtimes.

articleTitle: On stimulating productivity in the U.S.: The need to encourage innovation is broadly supported, and a program is sought
abstract: Technological innovation is the application of the industrial arts and sciences, along with the human intellect, to change the way society creates its goods and services, or the very nature of those goods and services. Despite the fact that technological innovation can secure large benefits for society, and that small businesses secure those benefits out of all proportion to their size, the rate of creation of small businesses in the United States has fallen dramatically over recent years. From 1964 to 1974, the number of new public issues for small high-technology companies dropped from $349 million to $6 million. Even more tragic is the fact that in the first half of 1975, there was not a single new issue for a small high-technology company.
In June, we noted that next year will mark the centennial of the electric light bulb, and we called for information from readers having personal recollections related to Thomas A. Edison.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Designer immersed in pool solar-heating project
abstract: The appeal of most of today's solar heating systems for the home transcends their present economic worth, according to one microprocessor designer who is nevertheless enthusiastically investigating one system he does feel to be cost-effective

articleTitle: Spectral lines: More power to you and more computer power, too
abstract: A careful study of the technical-interest profiles of IEEE's 180 000 members suggests that not quite 30 000 of them are linked directly and principally to the electric power industry " yet all members have a vested interest in energy matters simply by being consumers of power. Thus, it is not surprising to find, over the past few years, that articles published in Spectrum on the topics of power and energy have regularly garnered an impressive share of reader votes. Moreover, those areas of electrotechnology representing an overlap between the electrical and electronics arts " and, indeed, representing an overlap among the electrical, electronics, and computer arts and sciences " are consistently growing. Computers, in particular, are being exploited more and more by the utilities.

articleTitle: Productivity III: Management to the rescue
abstract: Despite some earlier analyses suggesting the contrary, management and labor have demonstrated time and again the validity of the old adage that where there is a will, there is a way - in this case, to increase productivity. Behind the various strategies described in this section is the recognition that technological innovation, if it is to be completely successful, must be nurtured and protected as it evolves through several stages. Hurdles will appear at the point of conception, through development, in production, and last, but hardly least, in the marketplace.

In mid-1977, when the project that culminated in this special issue first really began, skeptics found it difficult to believe that many significant new developments and applications involving electrotechnology could be unearthed. Yet by the time Spectrum editors had pored through the contributions of scores of industry consultants and numerous members of IEEE's Groups and Societies, it was clear that this skepticism was unfounded.

articleTitle: Texas Instruments' short-term `Idea' programs and its long-shot `Wild Hare' programs stimulate the company's innovators
abstract: People make innovations. But one has to create an environment in which people will be stimulated to innovate. And what few of us realize is that one can actually plan and organize systems to spur innovation.

articleTitle: Most are hardened skeptics, yet production workers may be guided to higher productivity and greater job satisfaction
abstract: What makes workers want to do a good job? The answer, if indeed one relatively straightforward explanation can be found, has thus far proved most elusive. However, elaborate theories, often extrapolated from seemingly successful case histories, abound. Money, promotions, status symbols, working conditions, peer-group pressure, pride, teamwork, enrichment programs... all have been thought to provide the key, yet each is but a single dimension of an intriguing social and political landscape that shapes attitudes and thereby individual actions.

articleTitle: Classic examples show how the Government can influence, directly or indirectly, innovation and productivity
abstract: Because the technological innovation process is so complex, ranging from basic research to the retirement of old technology, it is influenced by a broad spectrum of public policies. At times, this influence is intentional; in other cases, it happens indirectly — when intentional, technological opportunity, societal (market) needs, and timing have combined in such a way that public policy initiatives have contributed significantly to ultimate success.

articleTitle: Transportation: Electronics galore: Microprocessors broaden impact onland, sea, and air transport
abstract: The use of electronics is leading to many improvements in ground, air, and marine transportation. In both hardware and software areas, important steps are being taken to upgrade service, increase safety, cut costs, conserve energy, and reduce pollution.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Electronics and power: A remarriage
abstract: If, a few decades ago, the electronics engineer and the power engineer were little interested in one another's problems, and saw little need to be, such is hardly the case today. We pointed out in this column in February that all of IEEE's members have a vested interest in power just by virtue of being consumers. Beyond that, we noted, those areas of electrotechnology representing an overlap between the electrical and electronics arts are consistently growing. And the computer is dominant in this growth. Indeed, if there is to be a remarriage of electronics and power, the computer will probably be the matchmaker.

articleTitle: Amateur radio: OSCAR (and friends): Useful yet frugal: Since 1961, amateur radio operators have been launching satellites for communications, educational, and humanitarian applications
abstract: It happened one night in Little Rock, Ark. The huge animated neon sign of the Holiday Inn Hotel blinked and then went dark. A small group of people huddled in the parking lot. One person, a college student, pointed a compact VHF Yagi antenna skyward as the others watched. Shades of Close Encounters! “Where's the spacecraft?” someone asked.

articleTitle: The U.S. Activities Board of IEEE recommends actions Congress could take on behalf of the U.S. technologist and businessman
abstract: What can Congress do to spur U.S. productivity? The question was addressed in the writer's May 16 statement to the U.S. Senate Subcommittees on International Finance and on Science, Technology, and Space, in testimony on behalf of the Task Force on U.S. Innovation in Electrotechnology of the Institute's U.S. Activities Board (USAB). The following is an excerpt from that statement.

articleTitle: Best bits: applications of microprocessors: micros to probe jupiter...
abstract: NASA's deep-space Jupiter probe to be launched from the Space Shuttle will be a multiple first for microprocessors. If the barrel-shaped dual-spun “Galileo” satellite survives its 20-month trip and some 10 to 12 orbits around Jupiter, then it will be the first successful use of a micro in deep space and the first to survive high radiation - some predicted 1560 kilorads - courtesy of Jupiter's radiation belts, even with elliptical orbits about that planet to cut the dosage.

articleTitle: The computer in research: a real-time partner [Information services]
abstract: Discusses on-line information services with a survey of engineering data bases available in 1978 and an advice for inexperienced searchers.

articleTitle: Applications literature: IC design methodology and applications explained
abstract: This package of three applications notes covers worst-case design for ICS, ic log/lin multipliers as audio sweep function generators, and IC crystal oscillators combined with custom IC technology. All writeups introduce Interdesign's monochip concept.

articleTitle: Applications literature: Making measurements with piezoreslstive strain gages
abstract: This 20-page bulletin gives a detailed description of piezoresistance in semiconductors, strain-gage characteristics, and typical strain-gage measurement circuits. Definitions of piezoresistivity, gage factor, and doping start the presentation, followed by a discussion of gage characteristics. The circuitry section details bridge circuits, dynamic strain measurements, static strain measurements, gage factor compensation and maximum excitation voltage. Strain-gage installation is also detailed regarding surface preparation, cements, bonding bare gages, and bonding encapsulated gages

articleTitle: Power/energy: A rational approach to power plant siting: A technique that integrates economic, environmental, and site-specific data could result in better decisions
abstract: The selection and approval of sites for power-generating facilities has become extremely complex, lengthy, and costly. Utilities, regulators and rate-payers alike suffer most when regulatory proceedings impose delays after financial commitments have been made and construction has begun. One response has been to create analytical tools that may be applied earlier to help identify and begin to resolve controversial environmental issues.

articleTitle: Applications literature: Technical tips on creating PC artwork
abstract: This 121-page catalog and technical manual contains hundreds of work- and money-saving ideas on creating professional printed-circuit artwork masters. Topics covered in the manual include PC board documentation, electronic circuit diagrams, layout considerations, registration techniques, handling and storage of finished artwork, assembly drawing, and a selected bibliography of books, specifications, and standards. In addition, helpful tables and figures show conductor spacing minimums, recommended terminal areas, conductor-width processing tolerances, graphic symbols, and a listing of class designation letters used in the assignment of reference designations for electrical and electronic parts.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Productivity: Its ups and downs
abstract: Concern about productivity is universal among the highly developed nations of the world. Productivity in the United States, measured in the traditional way (value of goods and services divided by the hours of work required to produce them), rose only 1.6 percent per year, on average, from 1967 to the present, compared with 3.2 percent per year from 1946 to 1966.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Micro-pyramid may break time-share bottleneck
abstract: Time-share system designer, David Chung, architect of the F8 microprocessor and more recently a founder of Umtech, the home computer firm, has decided a resource-sharing home computer network is inevitable. He is seeking converts, both in private conversations and in a WESCON '78 paper.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Three amazing micromice: Hitherto undisclosed details: A closer look at some off the "smart" electronic micromice that have participated in the Spectrum/Computer Amazing Micro-Mouse Maze Contest
abstract: When Spectrum launched the Amazing Micro-Mouse Maze Contest in May 1977, it scarcely anticipated the deluge of entries (some 6000 to date). Thus far, three preliminary time trials have been held, during which several contenders entered the maze and failed to negotiate it or were scratched prior to post time. Evidently the design and construction of an intelligent mouse have proved less trivial than some had thought.

articleTitle: Productivity I: Defining the game and the players
abstract: Who's worried about productivity? We all should be, if we're to believe IEEE Fellows J. Fred Bucy (p. 45), Jacob Rabinow (p. 48), and Jordan Baruch (p. 47). These three men operate in vastly different environments with equally diverse concerns. Dr. Bucy, as president of Texas Instruments, is a “captain of industry” Dr. Rabinow, chief research engineer at the National Engineering Laboratory for the U.S. National Bureau of Standards, is one of the great, independent inventors; Dr. Baruch, Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Science and Technology, has much to do with the development of governmental technology policy. But all three agree that the future of innovation is in peril.

articleTitle: Exploding a few myths about productivity and presenting a formula for the future
abstract: There is ample evidence that in the past 17 years annual gains in productivity in the United States have lagged behind those of other advanced industrialized countries. Between 1960 and 1977, the U.S. could boast productivity increases of only 2.8 percent per year, compared with 5.7 percent for West Germany and 8.4 percent for Japan (Fig. 1). However, it should also be emphasized that the absolute productivity level in the U.S. is still high compared with other countries, even though the rate of improvement may be lower.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Registration: A second look
abstract: “The matter of registration of engineers as provided in the IEEE US Professional Activities policy has given rise to much questioning; and the membership is about equally divided,” President Ivan Getting reported in the January issue of The Institute. That portion of the membership not wholeheartedly in favor of mandatory registration questions it on two points: (1) Is it necessary for all engineers? (2) Might it become a mechanism for artificially and unduly restricting the practice of engineering?

articleTitle: How to improve the U.S. patent system, and encourage the `middle level' inventor
abstract: An invention is both an artistic and an economic phenomenon. An elegant invention, like anything else that is elegant, is truly a form of art. But any invention is influenced by the technological and economic climate.

articleTitle: Military: The U.S. Navy bets on V/STOL: Integrating technological advances on a broad front is the key to successful vertical/short takeoff and landing aircraft
abstract: The U.S. Navy has begun planning for the next generation of sea-based aircraft, which could revolutionize naval aviation. Termed V/STOL, for vertical/short takeoff and landing, these aircraft would be capable of operating from most types of naval vessels by taking off either vertically or conventionally within the confines of a comparatively short runway.

articleTitle: Productivity II: Electrotechnology to the rescue
abstract: Productivity is a complex measure. The factors affecting it involve substitutions and equivalents. For example, Texas Instruments' Patrick Haggerty has postulated that a “unit” of electronics (the “active element group”) can replace a given amount of energy that would otherwise be required in specific manufacturing operations. And, as Associate Editor Kaplan states in the introduction to his article, every fluctuation in availability and price of energy affects both the world economy and national productivity.

articleTitle: Techniques that optimize the use of the world's dwindling energy supply inevitably affect productivity as well
abstract: Energy — an inescapable input in all products and services — is becoming scarcer and more expensive. Every fluctuation in availability and price affects the world economy, in general, and national productivity growth rates, in the specific. Just how to make the most “productive” use of energy resources is therefore a subject of great importance.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: Tuneup for Detroit: New auto radios are rolling along in GM, Ford, and Chrysler products as electronics replaces mechanical tuners
abstract: Frequency-synthesized AM/FM electronic tuning is the latest word in automobile radios as Detroit's “big three” apply the state of the art in phase-locked loops, varactor tuning, and calculator-type logic. The main advantages are increased tuning accuracy, a virtually complete lack of frequency drift caused by temperature and voltage variations, and a potential decrease in both size and weight. The main disadvantage, at present, is price.

articleTitle: Education: Heavy readers are heavy hitters: A survey of 3000 RCA engineers not only reveals how they keep abreast, but correlates their information-retrieval habits with achievement
abstract: How do you see yourself? Would you classify yourself as a high or low achiever? And does your self-image correspond with what you want to be and what you'll actually do to attain that goal?

At times it seems the world is populated by two types of folks, systems thinkers and artists. Artists, the theory goes, act only upon instinct, while systems thinkers act logically or not at all. One might suppose that engineers (and physical scientists) are, per se, systems thinkers. Not so. There's a bit of artist in all of us, and some engineers, alas, appear to do their best work in a disorganized, unsystematic, and chaotic mode. Perhaps they are the geniuses among us. And a surprising number of others eschew even the simplest of systems methods (a checklist for the day's chores, for example).

articleTitle: Loch Ness revisited: Fact or fantasy? Science uses sonar and camera to probe the depths of Loch Ness in search of its resident monster
abstract: Underwater observations of moving targets in Scotland's Loch Ness, using sonar and photographic equipment, have heightened scientific speculation that the celebrated resident monster, “Nessie,” may be more than a tall tale. After centuries of myths, hoaxes, and unsubstantiated claims, there seems to be some basis for the cautious change in attitude that is taking place within the scientific community. Evidence gathered over the last decade has been largely responsible for this shift.

articleTitle: Applications literature: All about analog multipliers
abstract: This 40-page applications guide covers analog multipliers, dividers, squarers, and square rooters. Over 30 applications are presented, along with a section on theory and a bibliography. Applications detailed include increased accuracy with multiplying DACs, audio power boosters, bridge linearization, automatic level control, flow meters, and acoustic thermometers.

Index Terms: Years Of Experience In The Field

articleTitle: Computers: Consolidating gains: Solid-state progress is tempered by design maturation
abstract: The slowing and maturing trend in computer technology that became evident during 1976 was even more pronounced in the following year. Computer-aided design and software engineering made significant progress, and fault-tolerant techniques continued to advance toward their goal of ultrareliable systems. The major story in memory systems appears to be that traditional technologies such as cores, tapes, and disks are showing surprising resiliency and the ability to sustain continued improvement. Bubble memories and charge-coupled devices seem destined to play their expected roles, particularly in 10-100-Mbyte applications, but dramatic improvements are foreseen in the traditional memory technologies as well.

articleTitle: In praise of the small company and the technical manager as innovators: They're not afraid to take a chance
abstract: New companies in high-technology fields tend to be more innovative than the large, mature companies — and they also have other characteristics that are desirable to the economy. In the United States, for example, Science Indicators 1977 shows that from 1953 to 1977 an R&D dollar spent by a company with fewer than 1000 employees produced 25 times as many innovations as a dollar spent by a company with more than 10 000 employees.

articleTitle: Operating under stress and strain [electrical power systems control under emergency conditions]
abstract: In the U.S. today, complex power systems are able to provide reliable electric service at low cost with the help of automatic control - simultaneously tracking the randomly varying system load, optimizing generation to minimize cost, and coordinating the action of many independent control centers. When an emergency develops in one of these systems, however, the picture changes completely and new control objectives must be met if the system is to be restored successfully to normal operation.

Because more devices for customer generation and storage of energy will be in operation by the year 2000, the customer - residential, commercial, or industrial - will be considered a vital part of the electric power systems of the future. New types of central-station generation, storage, transmission, and distribution will be available, and there will be basic changes in the total energy picture as well.

articleTitle: Power: Whys and wherefores of power system blackouts: An examination of the factors that increase the likelihood and the frequency of system failure
abstract: Serious power interruptions or blackouts occur at the rate of about 35 per year in the United States, or about once every ten days somewhere in the country. And about half of these, on the average, exceed 100 MW and involve 45 000 customers at a time. In fact, the number of reported outages appears to be increasing at a rate of 6 percent per year. On the other hand, that rate is about equal to the average growth in served load over the same period. Further, despite all the publicity, and the damage that has been caused by individual incidents, the major reported interruptions represent only about 100 GWh per year of unserved energy. Compared with the 2 million GWh generated in the U.S. during 1976, this loss amounts to just 50 parts per million — a remarkable record.

articleTitle: Power/energy: System security: The computer's role: Several security-related functions can be aided by the digital computer, and linked together by a software scheme
abstract: Can computers in power-system control centers prevent blackouts? The answer is yes — and no. Apparently they cannot control a power system so that it will not become unstable. However, they can provide substantial help to the human who is operating the system. In addition to their contributions to various operational functions (see box on p. 50), computers assist the operators in preserving the system's security — its freedom from danger or risk.

articleTitle: Anatomy of a blackout: How's and why's of the series of events that led to the shutdown of New York's power in July 1977
abstract: On a warm evening last July 13, an intense electrical storm accompanied by heavy winds and rain moved southeast across Westchester County in the state of New York. At approximately 8:37 p.m., lightning struck the towers on a section of the right-of-way between two power transmission stations of the Consolidated Edison system, which serves the boroughs of Manhattan, Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island , and most of Westchester County. Less than 20 minutes later, other towers were struck. These two lightning strokes initiated a chain of events that led to the shutdown of the electrical supply for the city of New York.

The needs of television broadcasters and other communications professionals to store and then rapidly retrieve extremely large quantities of video information (e.g., text or moving pictures) are growing rapidly. However, it now appears that further large improvements in magnetic recording will be increasingly difficult to obtain. An alternative high-speed, mass-storage medium is required that is economical, compact, and archival. Random-access capability will also be necessary.

articleTitle: Communications: Spot beams promise satellite communication breakthrough: Focused antenna beams with frequencies accessed by time division can mean higher uplink power and more powerful communication service
abstract: In satellite communications, wide-area coverage and high antenna gain are generally mutually exclusive. For wide-area coverage, the emerging technology of time division multiple access (TDMA) utilizes a satellite's resources very efficiently, but at a cost of straining today's satellite technology to improve signal gain. High antenna gain is possible using another emerging technology, spot-beam antennas, but their coverage is limited to smaller geographic areas. Now a technique has been found that uses TDMA to provide high antenna gain over a wide area of coverage. This technique is called scanning spot-beam antennas.

articleTitle: Integrated optical spectrum analyzer: an imminent `chip'
abstract: The dramatic impact of the electronic integrated circuit upon virtually every kind of system has provided the justification for efforts directed at developing integrated optical circuits. Many of the same system benefits are expected to be realized for a variety of signal-processing and sensor functions - for example, reduced equipment size, weight, and ultimately, cost.

articleTitle: Displays: Flat-panel displays: A critique: They face six hurdles in displacing the CRT: Matrix addressing, duty cycle, luminous efficiency, uniformity/gray scale, color, and cost
abstract: Since the mid-1950s many researchers have forecast displacement of the cathode-ray tube by newer, “solid-state” flat-panel displays. Today, such forecasts seem even less likely to come true than they did 20 years ago. Over the years, the CRT and flat-panel displays have improved, but flat-panel-display problems have proved to be more formidable and fundamental than were realized. Rather than displacing CRTs entirely, flat-panel displays seem destined to compete strongly with them for certain applications — as in alphanumeric displays of 100 to several hundred characters.

articleTitle: Solid state: An update: CCD and bubble memories: Commercial units include 64-kbit charge-coupied-device and 92-kbit magnetic-bubble memories
abstract: Last year's emergence of both a single-chip 64-kbit (Ik = 1024) charge-coupled-device (CCD) and a 92-kbit magnetic-bubble memory (MBM) represents a leading edge of new memory-product developments. Already, laboratory design concepts and technologies are being aligned to create the next generation of these solid-state circuits. Concurrently, longer-range advanced laboratory programs are anticipating charge-coupled and magnetic-bubble memories in the multimegabit range by the early 1980s.

articleTitle: Solid state: Large-scale integration: Intercontinental aspects: Factors affecting the competitive positions of U.S., Japanese, and European firms include current business and economic climates
abstract: Ever since the invention of the integrated circuit (IC) and the silicon planar process, semiconductor producers in the United States have dominated the world markets for ICs, especially at the leading edge of each new generation of technology. This is certainly the case today for products of large-scale integration (LSI) complexity. But there are increasing signs that things might be changing.

articleTitle: Computers: A second chance for computer-aided instruction: What networking promised but didn't deliver may be developed at the local level as hardware costs drop
abstract: The lure of computer-aided instruction (CAI) is once again being felt by those who have maintained their interest in this problem-ridden educational tool and believe that advances in the technology will give it another chance. In the late 1960s, it was supposedly going to revolutionize the learning process; the best teachers were going to write "courseware" (interactive educational computer programs) that would be nationally distributed. Students would learn rapidly and efficiently. However, reality turned out to be quite different from the dream - so far.

In computer-aided instruction (CAI), the goal is to replace the traditional student-teacher dialogue with a student-computer interaction. Because machines communicate faster than humans, they should be able to provide more, and better, communication. This objective has been achieved in drill and practice, and in other narrowly defined circumstances - for example, classes for sales personnel and aircraft- and weapon-systems training. However, these circumstances represent only a fraction of all educational environments. In the vast majority of cases, CAI has yet to show results comparable to those associated with an experienced human teacher, even when exceptional programming material has been available.
Between the lines: Glossed over at hiring time, mandatory assignment agreements usually favor the employer. But sometimes they can be negotiated.

articleTitle: Power: Hardware and software for system protection: A survey of control techniques that minimize both the occurrence and the duration of blackouts
abstract: Since the 1978 Con Edison blackout in New York City there has been a growing awareness of the need for planning engineers to concern themselves not only with preventing such outages more effectively, but with reducing their duration. Mechanical controls that determine the behavior of steam turbines and generators must be considered in addition to electrical controls in the event of system faults.

articleTitle: Avionics: Microwave landing systems: As MLS technology enters its third decade, competing approaches contend for standardization at the international level
abstract: In the world of aviation, Microwave Landing Systems (MLS) have long been regarded as the preferred alternatives to the present international VHF/UHF Instrument Landing Systems (ILS) developed during World War II. The microwave system readily overcomes the major drawbacks of ILS - among others, limited number of frequency channels, difficulty in finding suitable ground sites at some airports, and susceptibility to interference by severe signal-multipath conditions. But though microwave landing sytems have found use, predominantly in military applications, they have yet to be applied to civil aviation to any great extent.

articleTitle: Military: Electronic warfare: From RF to EO: Electrooptics gains on RF and acoustic technologies in electronic deception, jamming, and neutralization
abstract: The importance of electronics in modern combat was dramatically demonstrated in the October 1973 Middle East war, when the Israelis used U.S.-developed chaff rockets to evade about 50 Russian Styx antiship missiles fired at them by combined Arab forces. In 1967, without such electronic warfare (EW) countermeasures, the Israelis lost a destroyer, the Eilat, and a merchant ship, both of which were sunk by Styx missiles.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Nimbus: The vanguard of remote sensing: Imaging and spectral analysis devices aboard Nimbus-7 measure the earth's radiation, wind speeds, and pollution, from space
abstract: Armed with a highly developed array of remote sensors, space satellites provide mankind with a fresh view of the environment from an extraordinary vantage point. These spaceborne imaging and spectral analysis devices furnish meteorologists, geologists, and many other scientists with a wealth of accurate information that may be frequently updated. The Nimbus program is of particular interest here as it serves as a “proving ground” for remote sensors that eventually wind up in dedicated operational satellites such as the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite that is responsible for the cloud-cover photos used on every television weather forecast. Nimbus-7, launched last month from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Western Test Range at Vandenberg Air Force Base in California is the last in this successful series. It contains eight highly complex sensors (seven from the U.S. and one from Great Britain) that are improved versions of instruments flown on six previous Nimbus flights.

articleTitle: Satellite/energy: The Franklin Institute has high hopes for its big balloon: A mile-long hot-air balloon is proposed for space research and solar power generation
abstract: While imaginative proposals have been made for extensive orbiting space stations at enormous cost, relatively little attention has been given to an idea that predates the space age and might be a useful complement to the satellites. The idea is simple enough: high-altitude, hot-air balloons. Unlikely as this suggestion may seem at first glance, it is worth investigating. Properly developed, it could prove considerably less costly and more readily attainable in a relatively short time than the orbiting space station.

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: Diagnostic imaging advances; microprocessors aid laser systems, prostheses
abstract: Amid universal concern over ever-increasing health-care costs and growing concern over technology's effect on those costs, biomedical engineering continues to make significant progress. Techniques for various diagnostic imaging modalities are still in the limelight. Transmission computer tomographic (CT) scanners with faster scans and variations of scanning schemes have been introduced. Making their commercial debut last year were emission CT scanners that use positron-emitting radionuclides or radiopharmaceuticals injected into, or swallowed by, a patient to permit tracing of metabolic processes. And ultrasonic imaging was further refined with improved detectors and scanning techniques. As imaging techniques become more sophisticated, they push the state of the art in computers, array processors, detectors, and data storage.

articleTitle: Solid-state devices: Memories and microprocessors benefit from large-scale integration advances
abstract: In the development of devices and components of any kind, the basic drives have always been to increase speed, decrease dissipation, and heighten functional complexity. Now those basic drives seem to have taken on new forms and to lead to new directions as the semiconductor industry embarks on a major assault on the fundamental limitations of large-scale-integration (LSI) technology.

This $6995 digital time-base corrector provides on-line correction of time-base errors caused by uncorrected tape speed and stretch variations occurring in longitudinal instrumentation recorders. These time-base errors constitute a form of signal distortion that can easily obscure pertinent timing relationships or spectral features of the original signal.

articleTitle: A minority report: Experts look at some of the assumptions used in traditional measures of productivity and probe productivity's impact
abstract: The conventional wisdom about productivity generally consists, these days, of a lot of hand wringing about the terrible things that are about to occur because of the alleged decline in the rate of productivity growth. This point of view is well expressed by Edgar Weinberg in the previous article (p. 34), and will be taken up in detail throughout the rest of this issue.

articleTitle: Computers are making giant strides in automating production - but human decision making is still crucial
abstract: In the 1960s, computers were considered by many as an infallible future way of boosting productivity, since they worked faster and had more memory than humans.

articleTitle: Power/energy: EPRI looks inward, and ahead: The electric power research institute's senior staff, in a candid session, probes its programs and progress
abstract: The problem: How to get the most for the electric utility industry's research and development dollar. The answer, an ambitious and innovative one, was initiated by the utilities themselves when they founded the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) in 1973. EPRI's charter — to develop new and improved technology for environmentally acceptable production, transmission, and distribution of electric power to help the utility industry meet present and future electric energy needs.

articleTitle: Power/energy progress report: A pastiche of developments promises near and long-term applications
abstract: The world's most northerly generating station is operating in the Arctic; in warmer climes, large turbine-generators and reversible generator/motors intended for pumped storage are on line. New solid-state field-excitation systems for large generators are being implemented successfully and equipment designed to prevent subsynchronous resonance is performing well. In the laboratory, research continues on generators with superconducting field windings, on ultrahigh-voltage (UHV) transmission, and on “bundled circuits” for 345-kV transmission systems. And high-voltage dc (HVDC) has taken a major step forward in the United States, sparked by the energizing of the first long-distance system employing fully solid-state conversion.

articleTitle: New product applications: Four-digit, presettable up/down CMOS counter family offers a host of features
abstract: Designated the ICM7217/7227 series, this family of multipurpose CMOS, four-digit up/down counters offers a four-decade presettable up/down counter, settable registers and comparator, set-table count offset, a multiplexed LED display decoder/driver system, and multiplexed BCD outputs.

articleTitle: Applications literature: All about printers and plotters
abstract: This 28-page full-color brochure describes advantages, applications, and specifications of 47 printers, plotters, and printer/plotters. The brochure also covers new computer output aids.

The most striking aspect of electrical and electronics technology in the People's Republic of China is not where it is, but where it's headed and how fast it's moving. In general, the Chinese are about 10 to 15 years behind the West in this area, having started, effectively, in 1948. But the Government has called upon the people to equal or surpass the industrialized nations by 2000. Western visitors, including a recent delegation from IEEE, agree that the Chinese could do it - if they solve the problems of reconciling their ideology with their drive for modernization and overcoming the serious flaws in their research, industry, and, especially, educational systems.

articleTitle: New product applications: High-speed wide-band FET-input op amp operates from a single positive supply
abstract: This high-speed FET-input wide-band operational amplifier may be operated from a single positive power supply with the inputs at ground potential. The input common-mode voltage includes the negative power supply voltage. Output-voltage swing is within 300 mV of the power-supply rail voltages, for full-load conditions. It is within 50 mV of the power-supply rail voltages for small low-current loads.

articleTitle: Applications literature: Applying thermal analysis to electronics manufacturing
abstract: This 16-page booklet contains 20 application studies that demonstrate the usefulness of the three primary thermal analysis techniques: differential scanning calorimetry, thermogravimetric analysis, and thermomechanical analysis. A spectrum of parameters related to electronics manufacturing are characterized, including PC board composition, component encapsulation, and wire insulation.

articleTitle: New product applications: 12-bit D/A and A/D converters feature universal microprocessor interfacing
abstract: This pair of 12-bit, dual-in-line packaged D/A and A/D converters is available with all the necessary circuitry to interface to microprocessor systems. Although other 12-bit and lower-resolution D/A and A/D converters are available with microprocessor interface circuitry, this pair - the MN3500 D/A and MN5500 A/D - are the first 12-bit units with total interfacing capabilities, available in a dual-in-line package. Thus, designers using them need not purchase additional multichannel I/O boards and design interface circuitry, as they would normally have to do using other converters.

articleTitle: Applications literature: Using a logic analyzer to debug microcircuit systems
abstract: This four-page applications note discusses two common problems in debugging a microprocessor-based process control system: an interface fault and an intermittent system input error. In both cases, a logic analyzer is used to find and diagnose the difficulty, considerably reducing the time spent in prototype debugging.

articleTitle: Power/energy: A giant step planned in fuel-cell plant test: A demonstration program for a prototype 4.8-MW dc fuel cell is underway for New York's Consolidated Edison electrical system
abstract: The day when electric energy will be supplied by fuel cells has been brought a step closer to realization. In August, shortly after it was awarded a contract by the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Energy Research and Development Agency and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), the Consolidated Edison Company of New York began a joint Government/electric utility program to install and operate a prototype 4.8-MW dc or 4.5-MW ac fuel-cell module on its electrical system. The module is being manufactured by the United Technologies Corporation (UTC). This demonstration program is the first effort to apply the fuel-cell concept in a utility environment, and to quantify and evaluate benefits that might accrue to electric utilities and their customers through its use.

articleTitle: A call for focusing on productivity: It directly affects inflation, cost of living, job stability - and the quality of life
abstract: In a little noticed sentence in the 1978 Economic Report of the President of the United States, the U.S. Council of Economic Advisors states that the slowdown in productivity growth in the United States is "one of the most significant economic problems of recent years." The slowdown affects almost every major issue facing U.S. citizens - the U.S. trade balance, the expansion of inflation, the number of jobs available, the very quality of life. And yet, this phenomenon has attracted insufficient attention among the nation's policy makers.

The name of the game in consumer audio is stereo. Phonograph record manufacturers dropped monaural products from their catalogs years ago, and music lovers of all persuasions now find the FM band predominantly filled with stereo broadcasts. However, AM radio listeners are still stuck with obsolete monaural sound - not because of lagging technology, but because AM broadcasters showed little initial interest in stereo. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) tabled AM stereo proposals in the early 1960s to encourage the growth of FM stereo. But the situation is changing dramatically. The AM broadcasters now proclaim they need a stereo option to stay competitive with FM, and broadcast-equipment manufacturers are anxious to oblige. Five competing AM stereo systems are now before the Commission; one of them is likely to be proposed for commercial use later this year. Here's a look at all five candidates- and a challenge: Can you predict which system will be chosen, and why? Spectrum will make a summary of your comments public once the FCC has reached its own conclusions on the matter (see box, p. 31).

articleTitle: New product applications: Hand-held DMM/calculator manipulates, stores, and retrieves values in five registers
abstract: This hand-held 3½-digit multimeter and rpn (reverse-Polish-notation) calculator is fully controlled by a CMOS microcomputer chip. A 32-key keyboard provides more than 70 functions, and results are seen on an eight-digit liquid-crystal display. All readings are obtained using a single set of test probes.

articleTitle: Computers: Personal computers for the entrepreneur: Microcomputers can help meet payrolls rather than play star wars availability of applications software packages is the pacing item
abstract: All the ballyhoo about a user-programmable microcomputer in every home has about run its course. Consumers are still interested, but right now they relate mostly to computing systems and advanced video games that can be set up with a prerecorded program cartridge (Atari, Fairchild, VideoBrain). Programmable microcomputers are being purchased by hobbyists, educators, and small businessmen. However, kits are much less important than they were only 18 months ago. Commodore Business Machines, Intelligent Systems Corporation, Radio Shack, and others have marketed “turnkey” computer products for under $1000 — but the cost of peripherals and additional memory typically pushes this figure much higher before a useful computing system can be realized. Seeing the consumer as a reluctant spender in this price range, many former hobby computer makers have begun courting the small-business customer. Here's a look at recent hardware and software trends, highlighted by some examples of microcomputer applications in the small-business community.

articleTitle: New product applications: Solid-state programmable limit switch can replace cam-operated counterpart
abstract: This programmable electronic limit switch is designed for OEM and plant production equipment used in such industries as steel, packaging, bottle and can manufacturing, metal working, plastics, printing, pulp and paper, and materials handling.

articleTitle: Experts look ahead to the day of the full-blown computer-integrated automatic factory
abstract: Sweeping changes and rapid advances are taking place in U.S. industry at an ever-accelerating pace, characterized by new trends in labor and product markets. The devices, machinery, and processes of industry are continually being updated or replaced by more complex instrumentation and more sophisticated techniques. And the digital computer is helping industry automate functions to a degree not contemplated in the past.

articleTitle: Measuring risk, both technical and marketing, is an important step in launching successful innovative products
abstract: There are two primary factors of risk in product innovation — technical risk and marketing risk. Technical risk is the possibility that the new product will fail for technical reasons, either in laboratory and field tests or in actual use by the customer. Marketing risk is the possibility of failure in the marketplace even though the product is a technical success.

articleTitle: Applications literature: Comprehensive symbol list for analog and hybrid computers
abstract: This eight page reprint contains a set of standard graphic symbois for analog and hybrid computers , the result of several years of work by a special technical committee on standards wiihin the Society for Computer Simulation. Many of the symbols are presented in several forms; some in the time-honored template style, and the others in a style intended to enhance the efficiency of computer graphics. In each instance, the symbol is accompanied by a name, function (equation or truth table), and explanatory notes.

articleTitle: Meeting preview: ELECTRO '78: Beans, brown bread, and Boston: 36 technical sessions organized by Program Chairman Brian Dale's committee promise toothsome technical fare, too
abstract: With more exhibitors, and more floor space available for their product presentation than in the previous two years, ELECTRO '78 — to be held in Boston's Hynes Auditorium and Sheraton-Boston Hotel, May 23—25 — promises to surpass the successes of the first two ELECTROs, in Boston (1976) and New York (1977). Living up to its theme “Look Ahead,” ELECTRO '78 will have some 350 exhibitors in 662 booths (last year there were 315 exhibitors in 560 booths) and an anticipated attendance of 25 000 persons — fewer than last year's 26 293 New York attendees, but far ahead of 1976's 21 645 Boston attendance.

articleTitle: New product applications: Desk-top computers feature a 256-kbyte read/write memory and assembly language programming
abstract: These desk-top computers offer as much as 256 000 bytes of user memory and feature an enhanced Basic language and an assembly-language programming option.

articleTitle: Applications literature: How to cool electronic equipment
abstract: This 18-page booklet and accompanying one-hour cassette audiotape comprise a mini training course covering many practical aspects of equipment cooling, including conduction, radiation, evaporation, natural convection, forced-air, forced-liquid, and fan selection. The booklet is illustrated with many charts and diagrams.

articleTitle: New product applications: Self-contained microprocessor chip contains 1024 bytes of ROM and 256 bits of RAM
abstract: Designated the S2000, this mjerocomputer has 8192 bits (1k 8-bit words) of ROM and 256 bits (64 4-bit words) of RAM, as well as input/output lines and a clock oscillator - all on one chip.

articleTitle: New product applications: development `laboratory' provides in-prototype testing for five common microprocessors
abstract: The 8001 microprocessor development “laboratory” provides in-prototype emulation for many 8- and 16-bit microprocessors - including the 8080, 6800, Z-80, TMS-9900, and 8085. It is designed specifically for the developer of microprocessor-based systems who already has access to software development capability, but requires a test bed for hardware checkout and for integration of software and hardware.

articleTitle: New product applications: Two-board data-acquisition system for TM990 microcomputer operates with a single instruction
abstract: With a single instruction, the ASC1080 analog input board, which is electrically and physically compatible with the Texas Instrument TM990 microcomputer family, can initiate a conversion cycle on a specific channel, fetch the converted data, operate on that data, and store the result. A second board, the ASC1081 analog output unit, can also convert the input word to an analog signal, with a single instruction.
